question_details.description:
This question is synced with an identical question on Metaculus. The original question opened on 2023-05-17 15:19:00 and can be found [here](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/17100). This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

As of May 2023, US law does not restrict API or browser access to any Large Language Models (LLMs), such as GPT-4 (ChatGPT) or Google Bard. As the capabilities of such systems grow, and users learn more how to extract certain types of knowledge (e.g. how to enrich uranium or create Deep Fakes), one way US policymakers might address risks would be to restrict usage to those that are verified to be in the US.

A similar regime exists for Digital Rights Management for music & movies - access to music on Spotify or shows on Netflix or Prime Video may depend on your country of origin. (And people regularly use VPNs to pretend to be from some other place to access this content.) Copyrights and trade agreements more generally often have provisions for various countries, and some countries like China ban access to entire systems via firewalls.

This question asks about APIs, not browser or app usage, because APIs are the most flexible way to use large AI systems. (In April 2023, [Italy banned and then unbanned](https://www.theverge.com/2023/4/28/23702883/chatgpt-italy-ban-lifted-gpdp-data-protection-age-verification) ChatGPT's interface but not the API, which was decried as ineffectual.)

question_details.fine_print:
* "Powerful generative AI systems" refers to AI that can solve a wide variety of tasks, such as GPT-4, and DALLE-2. Systems that translate, do text -> audio or audio -> text, summarize, search, etc. will not count as "generative".  If unclear, admins will determine "powerful" by whether the AI is known to frequently generate things that typically bother governments, such as Deep Fakes or instructions to build weapons.

* "Restrict" here will be interpreted broadly. It could be by requiring AI owners to check IPs, like with DRM; it could be by requiring people to verify their identity to get API access tokens, like with KYC. Doesn't matter how easy it is to circumvent such restrictions such as via VPN.

* "Only people in the US" will be interpreted broadly, it may include Americans who are abroad, or include non-permanent residents who are visiting, or require some verification only Americans can get like Social Security numbers.

**Protecting Privacy in Both Prompts and Responses**
Large language models (LLMs) such as OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, and Meta's Llama have raised significant privacy concerns due to risks associated with both inputs and outputs. Input privacy risks include the inadvertent exposure of personal or confidential data—such as when Samsung employees leaked proprietary code via ChatGPT, a situation where data cannot be retrieved or deleted from external servers. OpenAI retains user conversations by default to train models, increasing exposure risks. Output privacy risks involve LLMs memorizing and regurgitating sensitive training data, including personal information like addresses and phone numbers, or leaking data from other users due to bugs—such as a ChatGPT flaw that exposed payment details and chat titles. Core privacy threats include re-identification (reconstructing identities from anonymized data), data leakage (unauthorized exposure), and memorization of private data, which undermines the 'right to be forgotten.' To mitigate these risks, organizations are implementing input guardrails like anonymization, access controls, and input filtering. Output guardrails include response filtering, differential privacy during training, policy-based refusals, and red-teaming to detect leaks. High-profile incidents—Italy’s 2023 ChatGPT ban over GDPR violations, Samsung’s internal AI ban, and U.S. FTC investigations—have driven global regulatory scrutiny. Recommendations for responsible deployment include adopting Privacy-by-Design, implementing robust input/output safeguards, complying with evolving regulations (e.g., GDPR, EU AI Act), conducting regular audits, and ensuring transparency and user control. Tools like Guardrails AI and AWS Bedrock Guardrails provide scalable, code-based guardrails to enforce privacy policies.
